opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, thanks for having me. This is something I think about a lot, partly because of my work on open models, so I'm biased toward openness, and I'll say that up front.

I think we should default to releasing models openly, including weights and, ideally, the data and training recipes, unless there's a concrete, demonstrated reason not to. Right now, a lot of the arguments for keeping models closed are speculative. People point to bioweapons or cyber risks, and those are worth taking seriously. But when you look at the evidence for the marginal uplift a model gives over what someone can already find on the internet or in a textbook, it's been pretty thin for most of the models we've seen so far. Meanwhile, the costs of locking everything up are very real. You concentrate power in a handful of companies, academics can't study the systems that are reshaping society, and you lose the whole ecosystem of people finding bugs, building safety tools, and fine-tuning models for their own languages and domains.

That said, I'm not saying "release everything, no questions asked." I think the responsible version looks like a few things. First, staged evaluation: before you release, you test for the specific dangerous capabilities people worry about, and you publish what you tested and how. Second, transparency. Even closed labs should be much more open about their training data, their evals, and their safety processes, because right now the public is basically asked to trust them. Third, the frontier is different from the rest. If a model is clearly pushing into new capability territory, it's reasonable for that release to be more careful and more gradual. But models a generation or two behind the frontier should almost always be open, because that's where most of the scientific and economic value for everyone else comes from.

There's also a geopolitical angle people are waking up to. If the U.S. ecosystem doesn't produce strong open models, people around the world will just build on open models from elsewhere, like the very good Chinese open-weight models we've seen. So being closed doesn't actually keep the capability from spreading. It just means you lose influence over the standards, the norms, and the tooling.

So my short answer is: open by default, rigorous and public evaluation before release, extra care at the true frontier, and much more transparency across the board, including from the labs that don't release weights.

r001.rationale: It rejects releasing everything without conditions and says frontier models warrant extra care, so it does not endorse open release for every model.

r002.rationale: It says models pushing into new capability territory should be released more carefully and gradually.

r003.rationale: It favors opening models a generation or two behind the frontier, but does not identify them as a mechanism for gradual diffusion into the real world.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that there isn't one right way, and the question is really about what we're optimizing for. My own bias is toward openness, and I'll explain why, but I want to be careful not to pretend it's free of tradeoffs.

The case for releasing models openly, meaning the weights are available so people can run them, study them, and build on them, is mostly about who gets to participate. If only a handful of labs can touch frontier models, then the research on how these systems actually work, the safety work, the evaluation work, all of it gets bottlenecked behind a few companies' priorities. Open weights let academics, startups, and independent researchers poke at the models directly rather than through an API that can change or disappear. A lot of what we actually understand about things like fine-tuning, alignment techniques, and failure modes came from people working on open models, because that's what they could get their hands on.

The counterargument, and it's a real one, is that once weights are out, you can't take them back. If a model turns out to enable something genuinely dangerous, whether that's biosecurity concerns or large-scale fraud, the open release is irreversible. So I don't think "open everything immediately" is the right principle either. What I'd push for is something more like staged, deliberate release. Labs should do serious evaluation before they ship, be transparent about what they tested for, and if there's a specific, well-evidenced capability that's dangerous, hold that back or delay. But the default should lean toward openness, and the burden should be on showing concrete harm rather than vague discomfort.

The other thing I'd say is that the release decision isn't just about the artifact. It's also about what you publish alongside it. Data, training recipes, evaluation results, even the mistakes. A lot of "open" releases are really just weights with a marketing blog post, and that's much less useful to the ecosystem than something where people can actually understand how it was built. So when I say open, I mean open in a way that lets other people learn, not just use.

r001.rationale: The response rejects “open everything immediately” and says dangerous capabilities may be held back or delayed, communicating that some models or capabilities should not be released openly.

r002.rationale: It advocates “staged, deliberate release,” with evaluation before shipping and delays for specifically dangerous capabilities.

r003.rationale: The response does not describe open models following behind leading closed models as a way to diffuse AI gradually.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to distinguish between making a model available to use and releasing its weights so anyone can modify it and run it themselves. Those are different decisions, with different benefits and risks.

My starting point is that openness is valuable. It lets researchers scrutinize these systems, lets smaller companies build on them, and gives people more control over the technology they use. I don’t think we should assume that a handful of companies should be the only ones who can develop powerful AI.

But I also wouldn’t say every model should have its weights released immediately. You want to evaluate its capabilities, understand what risks it creates, and potentially release it in stages. Once the weights are out, you can’t really take them back.

So I’d favor broad access, with the release process becoming more careful as capabilities increase. And that needs to include transparency about what was tested and what remains uncertain, so the public isn’t just being asked to trust the company releasing it.

r001.rationale: The response says not every model should have its weights released immediately.

r002.rationale: It recommends releasing models in stages and taking greater care as capabilities increase, communicating gradual release for more capable systems.

r003.rationale: It does not describe open models following leading closed models as a diffusion mechanism.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we should take a staged approach. There’s a lot of value in releasing model weights: researchers can study the systems, developers can adapt them, and people don’t have to depend on a handful of companies for access. But as models become more capable, we need to be more deliberate about what we’re releasing, because you can’t really take the weights back.

I’d want to see evaluations of the model’s capabilities and potential misuse, followed by broader access as we understand those risks. For some models, that could mean an open release right away. For others, it could mean starting with limited access or an API. And openness should include documentation, evaluation methods, and information about training—not just a file you can download.

The key is to make the decision based on evidence about a particular model, while preserving the ability for independent researchers to scrutinize it.

r001.rationale: The response recommends limited access or an API for some models, rather than open release for every model.

r002.rationale: It advocates a staged approach, with broader access as evidence about a model’s risks develops.

r003.rationale: It discusses open release and limited access but does not describe open models following leading closed models as a diffusion mechanism.
